title: Linux Permissions Deep Dive
description: Go beyond basic chmod with symbolic permissions, ownership, umask, ACLs, and special permission bits like SUID, SGID, and sticky bit.

tasks.prompt: In your Ubuntu home directory, you own the regular file deploy.sh with no special permission bits and no extended ACL. Use chmod with symbolic notation to add execute permission only for its group, leaving all other permission bits unchanged.
tasks.hint: Use chmod with group add execute: 'chmod g+x deploy.sh'
tasks.explanation: Symbolic chmod uses who (u/g/o/a), operator (+/-/=), and permissions (r/w/x). 'g+x' adds execute for the group.

tasks.prompt: In your Ubuntu home directory, you own the regular file secret.conf with no special permission bits and no extended ACL. Use chmod with symbolic notation to remove write permission only for others, leaving all other permission bits unchanged.
tasks.hint: Use chmod with others remove write: 'chmod o-w secret.conf'
tasks.explanation: o-w clears only the others write bit. The owner and group bits stay unchanged; because you own the file, sudo is unnecessary. This removes write access through the others permission class.

tasks.prompt: In your Ubuntu home directory, you own the regular file database.conf with no extended ACL. Use chmod with octal notation to set owner read/write, group read, others no permissions, and no special bits (640).
tasks.explanation: Octal 640 means owner gets rw- (6), group gets r-- (4), and others get --- (0).

tasks.prompt: As an ordinary Ubuntu user with sudo access, use chown to change only the owner of the existing app.log in your home directory to the existing account www-data. Leave its group unchanged.
tasks.explanation: A username without a colon changes only the owner. A trailing colon would also select the user's login group. sudo permits transferring ownership to another account.

tasks.prompt: As an ordinary Ubuntu user with sudo access, use chgrp to change the group of shared_dir in your home directory and all its contents to the existing developers group. This tree contains root-owned files and no symbolic links.
tasks.explanation: chgrp preserves owners while changing groups. -R visits the directory and its descendants; sudo permits changes to the root-owned files too.

tasks.prompt: In your Ubuntu Bash session, use the umask builtin to display the current shell's file-creation mask in octal format without changing it.
tasks.hint: Run the umask command with no arguments: 'umask'
tasks.explanation: umask without arguments prints the current shell's mask in octal. The mask clears bits from the permissions requested when creating a file or directory; it is not arithmetic subtraction and does not change existing files.

tasks.prompt: In your Ubuntu home directory, you own the regular file project.txt, which has no extended ACL. alice is another existing account. The acl tools are installed and the filesystem supports ACLs. Use setfacl to grant alice read and write, without execute permission, through a named-user ACL entry.
tasks.explanation: setfacl -m modifies access ACL entries. u:alice:rw adds a named-user entry for read and write. The default mask recalculation includes these rights; the file owner can change its ACL without sudo.

tasks.prompt: In your Ubuntu home directory, project.txt exists and you can access its directory. The acl tools are installed. Use getfacl to display the file's standard permissions and extended ACL entries.
tasks.explanation: getfacl prints owner, group, traditional permissions and extended ACL entries, including the mask that limits named-user and group rights. Inspecting the ACL does not modify it or require owning the file.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, /usr/local/bin/backup_tool is a root-owned regular binary executable on a filesystem that permits SUID. As an ordinary user with sudo access, use chmod to set its exact octal mode to 4755.
tasks.explanation: The leading 4 sets SUID and 755 sets rwxr-xr-x. On execution, this binary takes the owner's effective UID (root here). sudo is needed to change a root-owned file; Linux ignores SUID on shell scripts.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, /tmp/shared already exists and is a root-owned directory with no other special bits. As an ordinary user with sudo access, use chmod to make it world-writable and set the sticky bit with octal mode 1777.
tasks.explanation: 777 grants everyone read, write and directory search permissions. The leading 1 restricts removal or renaming of entries to their owner, the directory owner, or a privileged process. sudo allows changing this root-owned directory.
